name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,351

entries.clue: Explain tutor’s leaving one after scheduled time (9)

indicatorNotes.leaving: Something leaving goes out and stays out, so the letter named next is no longer in the word it came from.

blocks.note: to tutor somebody is to train them, and the clue hands the verb over in its -s form
one is the Roman numeral I, and that is the letter that goes
turning up after the scheduled time is turning up late

annotation.surface: A tutor walking out once the appointed hour has already gone by.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Explain' looks like an instruction to the solver and is the definition. The apostrophe hides a verb: read 'tutor’s' as what a tutor does rather than as something belonging to one.
annotation.definitionFit: To translate jargon into plain words is to explain it, the sense the verb keeps when no second language is involved.

entries.clue: Examine TV equipment in lab (4,4)

blocks.note: to examine a candidate is to test them
the tube is an old nickname for television, after the cathode-ray tube inside the set

annotation.surface: Checking over the television gear somebody has set up in a laboratory.
annotation.walkthrough: 'TV' reads as part of the laboratory's kit and is a word waiting to be swapped. The definition is the last three words, which is why the join between the two halves is easy to miss.
annotation.definitionFit: A test tube is the thin glass cylinder a reaction is run in, standard kit on any laboratory bench.

entries.clue: Range of letters appearing regularly in pangram (3)

indicatorNotes.letters appearing regularly in: Letters appearing regularly come at a fixed interval, so you take every second one of the word that follows.

blocks.note: pAnGrAm, taking the second, fourth and sixth letters

annotation.surface: The spread of the alphabet across a sentence built to use every letter.
annotation.walkthrough: A pangram is a sentence containing every letter of the alphabet, which is what makes 'range of letters' sound like a description rather than an instruction. The answer is a make rather than a general word.
annotation.definitionFit: An Aga is the heavy cast-iron cooker found in British kitchens, and a cooker of that kind is a range.

entries.clue: Part of play witnessed in the auditorium (5)

indicatorNotes.in the auditorium: The auditorium is where an audience sits to listen, so the word is taken as it reaches the ear and not as it is spelt.

blocks.note: to have witnessed something is to have seen it, and that word said aloud is spelt the other way

annotation.surface: Watching an incident unfold from a seat in the theatre.
annotation.walkthrough: The auditorium is doing sound-alike work rather than setting the location, and the whole clue reads as theatre to keep that quiet. A play divides into acts and each act into these.
annotation.definitionFit: A play is built out of scenes, the units an act is divided into, so one of them is a part of a play.

entries.clue: That said simultaneously (2,3,4,4)

blocks.note: the phrase that concedes a point and then pushes back against it: true enough, nevertheless
two things happening across the same stretch of the clock

annotation.surface: Two people coming out with the same remark at once.
annotation.walkthrough: Three words in the clue and no wordplay anywhere, which is the whole difficulty. A phrase this long usually means the grid is doing the work, so count the enumeration before hunting for letters.
annotation.definitionFit: At the same time means during the same moment, and it also opens a concession, which is the job 'that said' does in a sentence.

entries.clue: Femme fatale having no time at all for royalty (7)

annotation.definitionNote: Royalty is a mass noun covering royal persons collectively, and a setter may use it of a single one of them.

indicatorNotes.at all: 'At all' means not in any degree, so not one instance of the letter is allowed to survive rather than just the first.

blocks.note: a femme fatale is a temptress, the woman who lures a man to his ruin
t = time, the letter on a stopwatch, and 'no' strikes it out

annotation.surface: A seductress who has not a moment to spare for the royal family.
annotation.walkthrough: The deletion is plural: the long word carries two Ts and both have to go, which is what 'at all' is quietly insisting on. Leave one in and the count comes out a letter over.
annotation.definitionFit: An empress rules an empire in her own right or reigns beside the emperor, which makes her royalty of the highest rank.

entries.clue: Helpful advice for turning round depression (3)

indicatorNotes.turning round: Anything turning round ends up facing the way it came from, so the letters are written in the opposite order.

blocks.note: a tip is a small piece of helpful advice

annotation.surface: Passing on a useful hint about handling a bout of low spirits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Depression' is a hollow worn in the ground, not a mood, and it is the definition sitting at the end. 'For' only joins the two halves; every instruction in the clue is in the turn.
annotation.definitionFit: A pit is a hole dug or worn into the ground, which is a depression in a surface.

entries.clue: What American might wear in inferior clubs? (5,4)

blocks.note: pants is British slang for rubbish or second-rate, as in a pants performance
clubs is one of the four suits in a pack of cards

annotation.surface: An American dressing for a night out round some fairly grim clubs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clubs' offers nightclubs and means the card suit. The definition points across the Atlantic because the answer is the American name for what Britain calls a trouser suit, and the wordplay uses the British sense of its first word.
annotation.definitionFit: A pants suit is the matching jacket-and-trousers outfit named after the American word for trousers, so an American is who would be wearing one.

entries.clue: Form quartet taking part in charity performance (4)

indicatorNotes.quartet taking part in: A quartet is four, and taking part in something means being inside it, so four letters in a row are lifted out of the words that follow.

blocks.note: chariTY PErformance carries the letters across the gap between the words

annotation.surface: A four-piece band agreeing to appear at a benefit concert.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Form' is the definition and the mildest word in the clue, which is how a hidden answer slips past. The letters straddle the space between two words, and that break is what disguises them.
annotation.definitionFit: Type means a sort or kind, and so does form: a rare form of the disease is a rare type of it.

entries.clue: Most frugal place for spring break (7)

blocks.note: a spa is the town built around a mineral spring
a break from work is a rest

annotation.surface: The cheapest spot anyone could pick for a week away in spring.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spring break' is one idea in the surface and two separate pieces in the wordplay, with the join falling between them. The spring is water coming out of the ground rather than the season.
annotation.definitionFit: The sparest room or meal is the one with least in it, so it is the most frugal of whatever is being compared.

entries.clue: Immature boxer perhaps transfixed by popular supermodel? (3,2)

indicatorNotes.transfixed by: To transfix is to run something right through, so what is named next is driven into the middle of the word before it.

blocks.note: a boxer is one breed of dog, and an immature dog is a pup
whatever is in this season is what is popular

annotation.surface: A young dog rooted to the spot by the sight of a famous model.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boxer' offers a fighter and means a dog, with 'perhaps' owning up to the breed being only one example of the animal. The question mark admits the definition is an example too.
annotation.definitionFit: A pin-up is anyone whose photograph is worth putting on a wall, and a supermodel is the clue's example of one.

entries.clue: Further education’s limiting at that point (5)

indicatorNotes.limiting: To limit a thing is to set the bounds it lies within, so the words on either side are the edges and what sits between them is taken whole.

blocks.note: furTHER Education’s runs the letters together across the space

annotation.surface: The grumble that staying on at college narrows a person rather than opening them up.
annotation.walkthrough: Further education is the British name for college study after school, which lets the clue read as a complaint about it. The letters run straight across the space between the two words.
annotation.definitionFit: There points back at a place already named — leave it there — which is what saying at that point does.

entries.clue: Quite unexpectedly exposed better manners (9)

indicatorNotes.unexpectedly: What happens unexpectedly does not come out the way you were expecting, so the letters arrive in some other order.
indicatorNotes.exposed: Something exposed has had its covering stripped away, so the letters at each end come off and the middle is left standing.

blocks.note: five letters of fodder, handed over whole
the B and the R at the two ends come away, leaving four more letters to re-set

annotation.surface: Someone caught out and turning out, to everyone's surprise, to have better manners.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Exposed' is the quieter of the two instructions and reads as part of the story rather than as a trim. Nine letters have to come from somewhere and the first word of the clue supplies only five.
annotation.definitionFit: Etiquette is the settled code of polite behaviour a society keeps to, which is manners taken as a body of rules.

entries.clue: No good leaving church service yet (4,2)

indicatorNotes.leaving: What is leaving walks out of the word, so the letters named before it are missing from what remains.

blocks.note: evensong is the Anglican service sung at the end of the day
ng is the standard short form of no good

annotation.surface: Somebody with nothing good to say slipping out of church partway through.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Yet' is the definition and looks like a stray adverb closing the sentence. The two letters that go are the last two of the service, which is what leaves the remainder splitting into two words.
annotation.definitionFit: Even so means nevertheless — he was warned; even so, he went — and yet carries that same concessive sense.

entries.clue: Wealthy area felt fun somehow (8)

indicatorNotes.somehow: 'Somehow' leaves the manner open, so the letters end up in some order other than the one they were given in.

blocks.note: a = area, the letter the formula for a rectangle uses
seven more letters of fodder

annotation.surface: A rich neighbourhood that turned out to be a good time after all.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wealthy area' reads as one phrase and only the first word is the definition; the second is a single letter of the fodder. Seven letters of clue for an eight-letter answer is the sign that something small has joined them.
annotation.definitionFit: An affluent household has money coming in steadily and plenty of it, which is what calling someone wealthy claims.

entries.clue: Drunk expert bored by his children’s game (5,4,4)

indicatorNotes.bored by: To bore is to drill a hole right through something, so what follows goes inside the letters already put together.

blocks.note: blind drunk is drunk past seeing, and in British use blind carries that sense on its own
what is his is a man's
a buff is an enthusiast who knows a subject inside out, as in a film buff

annotation.surface: A tipsy specialist sitting through his children's game and finding it dull.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bored' means drilled through rather than wearied, and it is the one word holding the pieces together. The game is the one where a blindfolded player gropes after the others, the last word being the shove they get when caught.
annotation.definitionFit: Blind man's buff is the old party game in which one player is blindfolded and has to catch the rest, so it is a children's game by name.

entries.clue: Leave abruptly — no longer available! (4,3)

blocks.note: the mark printed in the middle of the clue is a dash, and the setter means it to be read as the word
a dish the kitchen has run out of is off

annotation.surface: A sharp instruction to clear out because whatever you came for has gone.
annotation.walkthrough: The punctuation is the wordplay, which is about as rare as a device gets: the mark between the two halves is one of the pieces. Read it as a pause and the clue contains no instruction at all.
annotation.definitionFit: To dash off is to go in a hurry with no ceremony about the going, which is leaving abruptly.

entries.clue: Doctor lets us fight (6)

indicatorNotes.Doctor: To doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters come out altered from the order they went in.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder

annotation.surface: A doctor giving two of us leave to have a scrap.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' at the front of a clue is nearly always the instruction rather than the person, and here it acts on the six letters that follow. 'Fight' at the end does no work but define.
annotation.definitionFit: A tussle is a rough scuffle, the sort of fight that is more grappling and shoving than blows.

entries.clue: Obesity and laziness primarily causing death (5)

indicatorNotes.primarily: What comes primarily comes first, so only the opening letter of each word beside it is wanted.

blocks.note: obesity is an excess of fat
the opening letters of the two words

annotation.surface: The standard medical warning that being overweight and idle will kill you.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Primarily' reaches back over two words rather than one, and taking a single initial leaves the count a letter short. The definition is the clue's last two words.
annotation.definitionFit: Fatal is the word used of anything that kills — a fatal dose, a fatal blow — so it says of a thing that it causes death.

entries.clue: Sweets for kids (5)

blocks.note: the British pudding of fruit puréed into cream, gooseberry being the classic one
to kid somebody is to string them along, and this is the same verb in the same tense

annotation.surface: Puddings put out for the children.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For' does all the misdirection, joining two halves that have nothing to do with each other: one a dessert, the other a verb. 'Kids' looks like the children at the party and is what somebody does to them.
annotation.definitionFit: A fool is a cold pudding of fruit folded into cream, so several are sweets; and to fool people is to kid them.

entries.clue: Insect fly caught (4)

indicatorNotes.caught: To catch what somebody says is to get it by ear, so the word is written down as it sounds rather than as it is spelt.

blocks.note: to fly from danger is to flee, and that word said aloud is spelt the other way

annotation.surface: A fly that somebody finally managed to catch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fly' is the verb for running away, not the insect the surface dangles, and the definition is already sitting at the front of the clue. Three words, with the last one asking for the change of spelling.
annotation.definitionFit: A flea is the small jumping, biting insect that lives on cats and dogs, so insect is the plain class it belongs to.

entries.clue: Dismiss constructive pieces about report’s conclusion (3,2)

indicatorNotes.about: Something put about a thing is wrapped round it, so the letters named first go on either side of what comes next.
indicatorNotes.conclusion: A word's conclusion is where it finishes, so only its final letter is taken.

blocks.note: Lego is the plastic brick children build with, pieces sold for construction
the final letter of the word

annotation.surface: Brushing aside the useful parts of a document because of the way it ends.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Constructive pieces' is the trap: it reads as helpful contributions and it is a brand of toy brick. To let an employee go is the employer's soft word for sacking them.
annotation.definitionFit: A company that lets an employee go has dismissed them, the euphemism used when somebody is being shown the door.

entries.clue: Source of metal club and blade we’re told (4,3)

indicatorNotes.we’re told: Being told a word means hearing it, so what is wanted is the spelling that matches the sound rather than the word itself.

blocks.note: an iron is one of the clubs in a golfer's bag
the flat end of an oar is its blade, and that word said aloud is spelt the other way

annotation.surface: A golfer's club and a rower's blade named in the same breath.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves of the surface are things with a handle, which is what holds the sentence together. The first piece is the metal itself, so the definition sits uncomfortably close to its own wordplay — it survives because what is defined is the source, not the metal.
annotation.definitionFit: Iron ore is the rock the metal is smelted out of, so it is where the metal comes from rather than the metal itself.

entries.clue: Oxford Dictionary of English Verse (3)

blocks.note: the initials of those three words, which is how that dictionary is referred to

annotation.surface: A reference book of English poetry from the Oxford presses.
annotation.walkthrough: The italics run to the end of the clue and make the whole line look like one title. Only the first three words are the title: the Oxford Dictionary of English is a real book and goes by its initials, leaving the last word to define.
annotation.definitionFit: An ode is a lyric poem addressed to its subject, so it is one kind of verse.

entries.clue: Dread part of reward being sent back (3)

indicatorNotes.part of: A part of a word is a run of its letters, taken as they stand rather than the whole word.
indicatorNotes.being sent back: Anything sent back returns the way it came, so the letters found are written in the opposite order.

blocks.note: rEWArd holds those three letters in its middle

annotation.surface: The fear that part of the prize money will have to be handed back.
annotation.walkthrough: Dread here is the reverent kind, the feeling a cathedral produces, rather than plain fear. Short answers hide their fodder inside a single word like this, with no gap between words to give the join away.
annotation.definitionFit: Awe is dread mixed with wonder, the fear something vast puts into a person rather than the fear of being hurt.

entries.clue: Release material for coverage in newspaper that’s complimentary (9)

blocks.note: to release a prisoner is to free them
a sheet is the length of cloth that covers a bed

annotation.surface: Putting out material so a paper that costs nothing has something to write about.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Coverage' is press coverage in the surface and a bed covering in the wordplay. The definition is the whole of the last four words, which is where 'complimentary' stops meaning flattering.
annotation.definitionFit: A freesheet is a local newspaper handed out rather than sold, and complimentary is the trade word for what is given away.
